articles.title: IMF’s Georgieva calls AI a slow-moving tsunami (again) for jobs as graduates feel the first hit
articles.desc: Georgieva’s framing of AI as both a demand and an investment shock lines up with this week’s hawkish Fed commentary, which also pointed to AI-driven capital spending as a source of persistent inflation pressure, strengthening the case that the AI boom keeps rates higher for longer. Her estimate that
articles.content: Georgieva’s framing of AI as both a demand and an investment shock lines up with this week’s hawkish Fed commentary, which also pointed to AI-driven capital spending as a source of persistent inflation pressure, strengthening the case that the AI boom keeps rates higher for longer. Her estimate that AI investment could add half a point to a full point to growth in advanced Asian economies supports regional equities and currencies tied to the tech supply chain, such as Taiwan, South Korea and Singapore. The warning that AI could shift income from labour to capital, and erode governments’ main tax base, adds a longer-term fiscal risk for heavily indebted sovereigns. The IMF’s World Economic Outlook on Tuesday is the next catalyst, with markets watching whether the fund upgrades its growth forecasts on the strength of AI investment or cuts them on the energy shock. --- Earlier: Broadcom CEO likens AI boom to a casino even as he targets $230 billion in chip sales --- The IMF sees AI holding up the world economy and slowly hollowing out its job market at the same time, and the newest graduates are first in line. Summary: IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called AI a slow-moving but lasting threat to jobs on the opening day of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok She said the IMF expects about 40% of jobs worldwide to be augmented, downgraded or eliminated by AI over time, with routine work already hollowing out while lower-paid jobs grow Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam said AI is already cutting demand for graduates’ first jobs; in Singapore, the share of new graduates in full-time work fell to around 74% from about 88% for the 2022 cohort Georgieva said AI investment is acting as a demand and investment shock that could lift growth in advanced Asian economies by half a point to a full point, helping keep global growth around 3% despite an energy supply shock She warned AI could erode taxes on labour, governments’ main revenue source, and urged policymakers to act now The IMF’s World Economic Outlook, with updated forecasts, is due on Tuesday International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence poses a lasting threat to jobs, describing it as a slow-moving but unmistakable tsunami as the IMF and World Bank annual meetings opened in Bangkok. Georgieva has used the tsunami comparison several times this year, but her latest remarks, reported by Bloomberg, added that the shift is unfolding gradually. She said AI is already reducing demand for routine, repetitive work while adding lower-paid jobs in sectors such as construction, an outcome she said was nothing to celebrate. The IMF expects about 40% of jobs worldwide to be augmented, downgraded or eliminated by AI over time. That estimate builds on IMF research first published in January 2024, which put exposure at roughly 60% of jobs in advanced economies, 40% in emerging markets and 26% in low-income countries. It also found that about half of exposed jobs in rich economies could benefit from AI rather than lose out. Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same meetings, said the first rung of employment, the first job after graduation, is seeing less demand, and that the evidence is clearest in the sectors most exposed to AI, Reuters reported. Singapore’s own data illustrate the point. Around 74% of its 2025 university graduates in the labour force found full-time work, down from about 88% of the 2022 cohort, while the share unemployed and seeking work rose to about 10% from under 4%, according to a Ministry of Education survey. The causes are still debated. A Harvard working paper found junior employment fell by about 9% at firms that adopted generative AI, relative to those that did not. A May 2026 study by researchers at the University of Warwick, the London School of Economics and Oxford found that much of AI’s apparent effect on junior hiring faded once exposure to remote work was taken into account. Georgieva also stressed that AI is supporting the world economy. She described the boom as a demand and investment shock that could lift growth in advanced Asian economies by between half a percentage point and a full point, Reuters reported, and said it is helping keep global growth around 3% despite an energy supply shock. She flagged a longer-term risk for public finances: by tilting economies toward capital and away from labour, AI could erode the taxes on work that have traditionally been governments’ main source of revenue. Georgieva urged policymakers to assess developments carefully and act on the lessons now. The IMF’s World Economic Outlook, with updated growth forecasts, is due on Tuesday and will show how heavily the fund is weighing AI investment against the energy shock. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis
articles.desc: Union urges Mayor to halt driverless taxi rollout as City Hall report raises questions about safety, congestion, and who's actually in charge
articles.content: London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis London cabbies want Sadiq Khan to slam the brakes on robotaxis Union urges Mayor to halt driverless taxi rollout as City Hall report raises questions about safety, congestion, and who's actually in charge BT Tower's rooftop pool plan brings swimmers back down to earth Wayve and Uber steal a march on Waymo with paid self-driving London rides 'Uber rapture' leaves passengers and drivers behind in Nigeria and Uganda Waymo has designed a robocar chip to stay ahead of Tesla More than half of Americans now view AI negatively London's minicab drivers want Mayor Sadiq Khan to put the brakes on robotaxis before they threaten thousands of jobs, with a new City Hall report casting doubt on whether the capital is ready for driverless cars. The Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB) has called on Transport for London (TfL) to halt the rollout following the publication of a The 66-page report makes uncomfortable reading for the companies hoping to unleash fleets of driverless taxis on London's streets. "As it stands, we currently have not heard sufficient evidence to persuade us that London should welcome autonomous passenger services," it concludes. Google's Waymo, British startup Wayve, and Chinese tech giant Baidu are among those gearing up to bring autonomous passenger services to London. Waymo has already been testing its cars in the capital and hopes to launch a commercial fleet of "low hundreds" this year, subject to regulatory approval. Uber and Wayve have secured TfL private hire licenses for vehicles offering supervised self-driving rides, meaning a human driver remains legally in control, and Freenow and Baidu are targeting a fully driverless launch in 2027. London has around 105,000 licensed private hire drivers, many of whom have reason to worry about cars that can do their jobs without them. "Every car feeds a family, and the prospect of not being able to earn money leaves us all with a deep uncertainty as to how we will provide for them. We already struggle to get by as it is," said Gholomreza "Rez" Kamyabi, an Uber driver and vice chair of the IWGB Private Hire Drivers union. The committee heard warnings that robotaxis could put large numbers of drivers out of work, and wants TfL to work with unions and operators to retrain, redeploy, and fund those affected. The IWGB, however, wants the rollout stopped. "The IWGB Private Hire Drivers Union opposes the rollout of driverless cars," said union president Alex Marshall, warning the technology could put thousands out of work while benefiting tech companies and investors. Jobs aren't the only concern. Under the government's interim Automated Passenger Services permitting scheme, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) issues operating permits. TfL must consent before a service launches in London, but cannot independently suspend or revoke a permit once issued. TfL also has no formal say over existing driverless trials, and operators aren't legally required to report incidents to it, although some have shared information voluntarily. The report details several incidents involving autonomous test vehicles, including a car reportedly entering a police crime scene cordon in April, another filmed turning the wrong way into a one-way street in June, and a reported collision with a motorcycle in July. It also questions how robotaxis would handle medical emergencies, passenger safety, and accessibility. None of the autonomous vehicles currently being trialed are wheelchair accessible. Then there's congestion. Robotaxis could lure passengers away from public transportation while adding more traffic as vehicles travel empty between fares. The committee wants operators to report their empty mileage so TfL can assess the impact. Londoners aren't exactly clamoring for the technology either. articles.title: “Not Accurate”: BCCI Denies Reports Of India vs Sri Lanka ODI Venue Shift From Delhi To Ahmedabad
articles.desc: File image of BCCI Secretary Devajit Saikia.© BCCI The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) Secretary Devajit Saikia dismissed reports claiming that the opening ODI between India and…
articles.content: "Not Accurate": BCCI Denies Reports Of India vs Sri Lanka ODI Venue Shift From Delhi To Ahmedabad - SwapUpdate File image of BCCI Secretary Devajit Saikia. The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) Secretary Devajit Saikia dismissed reports claiming that the opening ODI between India and Sri Lanka, scheduled for December 13 in Delhi, had been shifted to Ahmedabad amid concerns over ongoing construction work at the Arun Jaitley Stadium. Saikia said on Monday that no decision had been made to shift the fixture, reiterating that bilateral matches are allocated to venues in accordance with the BCCI’s standard policy. He urged the media to rely on official BCCI updates for accurate information. “Reports suggesting that the India–Sri Lanka ODI match scheduled in Delhi may be shifted to Ahmedabad are not accurate. There has been no such decision by the BCCI. We request media colleagues to kindly refer to official BCCI communications for any updates regarding the schedule. Further, it needs to be reiterated that bilateral matches are primarily allotted by following a standard policy,” Devajit Saikia said. The Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad is already slated to host the third and final ODI on December 19. Sri Lanka is scheduled to tour India from December 13 to 27, 2026, for a white-ball series featuring three ODIs and three T20Is. The ODI series will open in Delhi before moving to Bengaluru and Ahmedabad for the second and third matches, respectively. The teams will then face off in a three-match T20I series, with matches scheduled in Rajkot, Cuttack and Pune. articles.title: Eyring Movers Ranked Top Moving Company in Avon Lake and Vermilion by moveBuddha
articles.desc: Northeast Ohio's 129-year-old family moving company earns top marks across three independent moveBuddha rankings, including long-distance moves within Ohio.
articles.content: Eyring Movers Ranked Top Moving Company in Avon Lake and Vermilion by moveBuddha There were 1,553 press releases posted in the last 24 hours and 496,325 in the last 365 days. Eyring Movers Ranked Top Moving Company in Avon Lake and Vermilion by moveBuddha Northeast Ohio's 129-year-old family moving company earns top marks across three independent moveBuddha rankings, including long-distance moves within Ohio. Being ranked first by a platform that compares movers for a living is an honor, but what it really reflects is how our crews treat every family on every job.” AVON LAKE, OH, UNITED STATES, October 12, 2026 / serving Northeast Ohio since 1897, has been named the top-rated moving company in Avon Lake, Ohio by moveBuddha, the independent moving research and comparison platform. The company also earned the top position in moveBuddha's rankings for Vermilion and was rated the best Avon Lake-based mover for moveBuddha's rankings are built from verified customer reviews, Better Business Bureau ratings, and proximity to each community. In Avon Lake, the platform evaluated 24 local movers using 3,829 verified customer reviews, where the market average score was 4.42 out of 5. Eyring Movers earned a score of 4.5. In Vermilion, moveBuddha compared 15 movers serving the city, drawing on more than 16,000 reviews from across Ohio, and Eyring again ranked first with a 4.5 rating against a market average of 4.38. The third recognition carries particular weight for families relocating across the state. In its analysis of 99 Ohio moving companies, moveBuddha named Eyring Movers the top-rated Avon Lake-based mover for long-distance moves within Ohio, with a score of 4.56 out of 5. For residents moving from the Lake Erie shoreline to Columbus, Cincinnati, or anywhere in between, the ranking reflects the company's ability to deliver the same standard of care on a 200-mile move as on a move across town. "Being ranked first by a platform that compares movers for a living is an honor, but what it really reflects is how our crews treat every family on every job," said Brian Yarham, owner of Eyring Movers. "We have been moving Northeast Ohio for 129 years, and our reputation has always been built one customer at a time. These rankings tell us our customers are still seeing that." moveBuddha's review highlights clear communication, careful handling, and transparent deposit expectations as standout qualities. Across roughly 237 reviews, nearly all customer feedback for Eyring Movers is positive, with an average Yelp rating of 4.8. Eyring Movers holds a clean federal safety record as a licensed interstate household goods carrier under USDOT number 120489 and MC number 87872. The company provides local moving, residential moving, long-distance moving, , senior moving, piano moving, and storage services from four offices in Avon Lake, Lakewood, Strongsville, and Marblehead. Its Marblehead location also supports moves to and from Kelleys Island, Put-in-Bay, and Middle Bass Island, a service few Ohio movers offer. In 2024, Eyring Movers expanded its reach with the acquisition of Dussault Moving Company, a Lakewood mover founded in 1961, which now operates as Eyring Movers Lakewood and serves Lakewood, Rocky River, and Cleveland's near west side. Families and businesses planning a move in Northeast Ohio can request a free estimate at eyringmovers.com or by calling the Avon Lake headquarters at 440-653-5990. Eyring Movers (Edward Eyring & Sons, Inc.) is a family-owned moving and storage company founded in 1897 and headquartered at 638 Moore Road in Avon Lake, Ohio. With offices in Avon Lake, Lakewood, Strongsville, and Marblehead, the company provides local, long-distance, residential, and specialty moving services throughout Northeast Ohio and the Lake Erie islands. articles.title: Stellantis CEO is calling on E.U. to reward carmakers that build locally
articles.desc: Antonio Filosa says European-made cars should be protected by regulation as Chinese automakers expand their regional market share
articles.content: Stellantis CEO urges E.U. incentives for local carmakers Stellantis CEO is calling on E.U. to reward carmakers that build locally Antonio Filosa says European-made cars should be protected by regulation as Chinese automakers expand their regional market share CEO Antonio Filosa is pressing European regulators to do more to support carmakers that produce vehicles on the continent, as Chinese automakers deepen their presence across the region. "What we are supporting a lot in Europe is to establish for everybody a level playing field," Filosa told CNBC's Charlotte Reed in an interview ahead of the Paris Motor Show on Monday. "In concrete terms, it means to work on true regulation... starting from 'Made in Europe,' that should be regulation that incentivizes, rewards, and protects the ones that are able to demonstrate that they design cars, engineer cars." Made in Europe is a term for a proposed E.U. Commission policy that would set minimum thresholds for locally sourced content as a condition of market access, according to Chinese brands have expanded at a significant pace globally, with their worldwide auto-sales share climbing nearly 70% between 2020 and 2025, according to CNBC, citing data from GlobalData. Their share of European car sales has risen to 12% as of August, up from close to zero in 2020, according to CNBC, citing data from Dataforce. Filosa acknowledged the competitive threat, saying Chinese automakers "can really offer many consumers in many segments, good technology, and competitive prices." at an event ahead of the Paris Motor Show, including a revival of Citroën's 2CV — a European-made electric vehicle concept with a target price of €15,000 ($16,800), according to . The concept is expected to enter production in 2028 and represents the first example of a new E.U. category of low-cost EVs, Reuters reported. "This event brings our FaSTLAne 2030 strategy to life," Filosa said in a statement. "It reflects the extraordinary effort of our teams and our commitment to shaping the future of mobility through iconic brands, compelling design and innovative technology." stock has fallen about 60% so far this year. The company has been working through a turnaround strategy, and returned to quarterly profitability in the first three months of 2026 for the first time in over a year, posting €960 million in adjusted operating income. Net revenues for the quarter reached €38.1 billion, a 6% increase from the same period in 2025. European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said Friday that China had agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the E.U. bloc, according to CNBC. stock added 2.7% in early Monday trading following news of the agreement. articles.title: Appeal for major energy storage system rejected
articles.desc: Plans for the battery system site near the Devon-Dorset border have again been dismissed.
articles.content: Appeal for major energy storage system in Devon rejected - BBC News Proposals to install a major battery energy storage system have been rejected after an appeal by the developer was dismissed. Sky UK Development's plans for the battery system site (BESS) on land near Raymond's Hill in Axminster were refused by East Devon District Council's planning committee last year. The applicant appealed the decision with the Planning Inspectorate, proposing changes to mitigate concerns around groundwater contamination and the risk of battery units catching fire. In her decision, inspector RC Kirby said such mitigation "would not be effective" in ensuring an acceptable balance between harm and benefit", stating the proposal was "not suitable for its location". A key risk highlighted during the planning debate for the proposed BESS revolved around what could happen if one of the battery units caught fire, according to the Opponents claimed the amounts of water needed to contain such blazes and prevent their spread could mean any water running off into a nearby local waterway. The appellant said it believed it would be about eight years before water used to fight a notional fire at the BESS would reach the drinking water source, but the inspector said there had been "insufficient evidence" to substantiate this. The appeal decision notice stated the appellant had put forward revised plans that East Devon had not had put before it. These included an increase in the size of the water tanks, relocation of some of the tanks, the separation distance between pairs of containers being 6m (20ft) apart, and other alterations. Campaigners from Devon branch of the Campaign to Protect Rural England (CPRE) and the Hawkchurch and Monkton Wyld Action Group said they were "massively relieved" plans for the site had been blocked. Devon CPRE energy spokesperson Dr Phil Bratby added: "For years, Devon CPRE has been highlighting the risks from the hazardous materials that could be released and contaminate the groundwater." Kirby said that, while the benefits of the scheme would "outweigh the moderate harm that would be caused to the Dorset National Landscape", they were "insufficient" to outweigh the "very substantial, overriding, unacceptable risks in respect of pollution of the water environment". Proponents of BESS systems highlighted their benefits in helping the nation reach net zero aspirations, notably because they could store energy. The UK government noted BESS systems used batteries, for example lithium-ion batteries, to store electricity at times when supply was higher than demand. "They can then later release electricity when it is needed. BESSs are therefore important for "the replacement of fossil fuels with renewable energy", it stated.
